pages.title: Storage Engine Architecture
bulletPoints: Storage engines are the core components responsible for managing how data is stored on disk and in memory.
Primary categories: In-Memory engines vs Disk-Based engines; Mutable in-place engines vs Append-only log engines.
Components: Buffer pool manager, Lock/Latch manager, Write-Ahead Log (WAL), and On-disk indexing tree.
Trade-offs: Read amplification, Write amplification, and Space amplification (RUM conjecture).

pages.title: B-Tree Anatomy & Node Layout
bulletPoints: B-Trees: Balanced search trees optimized for block storage devices like SSDs and HDDs.
Node layout: Slotted-page architecture with cell pointers growing forward and cell data growing backward.
Fan-out: A high branching factor (typically 100 to 1,000 keys per node) minimizes tree depth to 3 or 4 levels.
Search complexity: O(log_B N) disk accesses, making B-Trees ideal for read-heavy transactional workloads.

pages.title: B-Tree Node Splitting & Balancing
bulletPoints: Insertion: Traversing down to target leaf node; if node overflows (capacity > 2B), the node splits into two halves.
Median key promotion: The middle key moves up to the parent node, potentially causing a cascade of parent splits.
Deletion: Removing key from leaf; if node underflows, borrowing keys from siblings or merging with neighbor nodes.
Right-leaning bulk loading: Constructing B-Trees sequentially from sorted data to achieve 100% space utilization.

pages.title: B-Tree Concurrency & Latching
bulletPoints: Locks vs Latches: Locks protect logical database transactions; Latches protect physical in-memory data structures.
Latch crabbing / coupling: Acquiring a child node latch before releasing the parent node latch.
Optimistic latching: Reading node versions without acquiring exclusive write latches to maximize concurrency.
B-link trees: Lehman-Yao algorithm adding sibling pointers to allow concurrent read traversals during ongoing node splits.

pages.title: LSM-Tree Architecture Overview
bulletPoints: Log-Structured Merge-Tree: Optimized for write-heavy workloads by sequentializing all disk writes.
Memtable: An in-memory sorted structure (typically SkipList or Red-Black Tree) accepting concurrent writes.
Commit Log / WAL: Sequential append-only disk log guaranteeing durability in case of server crashes.
SSTables (Sorted String Tables): Immutable on-disk sorted files flushed periodically from frozen Memtables.

pages.title: SSTable Anatomy & Block Indexing
bulletPoints: SSTable layout: Sequence of fixed-size compressed data blocks followed by an index block and footer.
Index block: Sparse primary key index mapping keys to file byte offsets for fast seeking.
Two-pass binary search: Searching the index block to find target data block, then searching inside the decompressed block.
Immutability advantage: No locks or latches required for read queries against historical SSTable files.

pages.title: Bloom Filters in LSM-Trees
bulletPoints: The read penalty of LSM-Trees: Looking for non-existent keys requires checking multiple SSTables on disk.
Bloom filter: Space-efficient probabilistic data structure answering whether a key is 'possibly in set' or 'definitely not in set'.
Hashing mechanics: k independent hash functions setting bits in an m-bit bitset array.
False positive rate: Configured to ~1% with just 10 bits per key, eliminating 99% of unnecessary disk I/O on lookups.

pages.title: Compaction Strategies: Size-Tiered vs Leveled
bulletPoints: Why compaction is mandatory: Reclaiming space from deleted/updated keys and bounding read latency.
Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS): Merging SSTables of similar sizes; great for write-heavy bursts, higher temporary space overhead.
Leveled Compaction (LCS): Partitioning disk into exponential levels (L0, L1, L2); each level has strictly non-overlapping keys.
Trade-off analysis: Leveled compaction yields predictable low read latency and minimal space amplification at cost of higher write amplification.

pages.title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) & Recovery
bulletPoints: The ARIES recovery algorithm: Analysis, Redo, and Undo phases for robust database recovery.
Write-Ahead Log rule: Dirty data pages in memory must never be written to disk until the corresponding log records are flushed.
Group commit: Batched fsync calls combining multiple concurrent client transactions into a single disk I/O.
Checkpoints: Periodic snapshots writing dirty pages to disk, allowing truncation of historical WAL segments.

pages.title: Buffer Pool Management & Page Eviction
bulletPoints: Buffer pool: In-memory frame cache holding 4KB/8KB disk pages to minimize slow storage I/O.
Page table: Hash map translating disk page IDs to memory buffer frame pointers.
Eviction algorithms: LRU (Least Recently Used), Clock-sweep, 2Q, and adaptive replacement caches (ARC).
Dirty page management: Background flusher threads writing modified pages to disk before evicting.

pages.title: Columnar Storage & Analytics Engines
bulletPoints: Row-oriented (OLTP) vs Column-oriented (OLAP): Storing tuples together vs storing attributes together.
Vectorized execution: Processing arrays of columnar values in CPU L1 cache with SIMD instructions.
Compression algorithms: Run-length encoding (RLE), Bit-packing, Delta encoding, and Dictionary compression.
Projection pushdown: Reading only the specific columns referenced in the query, cutting disk I/O by 90%.

pages.title: MVCC: Multi-Version Concurrency Control
bulletPoints: Core principle: Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.
Tuple headers: Storing created-by (xmin) and deleted-by (xmax) transaction IDs with each row version.
Read views / Snapshots: Determining row visibility based on the calling transaction's active snapshot.
Vacuuming & Garbage Collection: Identifying and purging dead tuple versions that are no longer visible to any active transaction.

pages.title: Distributed Storage Partitioning
bulletPoints: Horizontal sharding: Splitting large tables across multiple database nodes.
Range partitioning: Partitioning by key ranges (e.g. A-E, F-M, N-Z); prone to hot spot writes on monotonic keys.
Hash partitioning: Applying cryptographic hash functions (e.g. Murmur3) to distribute keys uniformly.
Consistent Hashing: Virtual nodes on a hash ring minimizing data rebalancing when nodes join or leave the cluster.

pages.title: Consensus Protocols in Storage: Raft & Paxos
bulletPoints: State machine replication: Replicating an identical append-only log across independent storage nodes.
Leader election: Heartbeats, election timeouts, and randomized split-vote prevention in Raft.
Log replication: Majority quorum acknowledgement before committing entries to disk state machines.
Safety invariant: A committed entry is guaranteed to be present in all future leader terms.

pages.title: Distributed Transactions & Two-Phase Commit
bulletPoints: Atomic commit across shards: Either all participating nodes commit the transaction or all abort.
Phase 1 (Prepare): Coordinator sends prepare requests; participants write undo/redo logs and vote YES or NO.
Phase 2 (Commit): If all vote YES, coordinator broadcasts COMMIT; otherwise coordinator broadcasts ABORT.
Failure modes: Blocking coordinator problem when coordinator crashes during the critical commit window.

pages.title: Modern Trends: NVMe, Optane & Memory Tiering
bulletPoints: Ultra-fast NVMe storage: Millions of IOPS and single-digit microsecond latencies changing engine assumptions.
Kernel bypass & io_uring: Asynchronous Linux I/O eliminating costly syscall context switches.
Persistent Memory (PMEM): Byte-addressable non-volatile RAM bridging the latency gap between DRAM and SSDs.
Vector databases: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes like HNSW storing high-dimensional embedding vectors.

pages.title: Database Architecture Synthesis
bulletPoints: Selecting the right storage engine: B-Tree for relational OLTP, LSM-Tree for ingestion logs, Parquet for analytics.
Balance of trade-offs: Memory bandwidth, disk write amplification, CPU cache locality, and recovery time.
Hardware alignment: Designing data structures that respect hardware page sizes and CPU cache line boundaries.
Future outlook: Cloud-native disaggregated architectures separating serverless compute from scalable object storage.
